sections.h2: Where is McKinley County, New Mexico, and who lives there?
sections.html:
McKinley County is in northwest New Mexico on the Arizona line, and Gallup is both its county seat and its only incorporated city. The county covers 5,455 square miles, bordered by San Juan, Sandoval and Cibola counties and by Apache County, Arizona.

The state labor department describes the county as overlapping the Navajo Nation and the Zuni Reservation, with over 60 percent of the land in those two reservation areas. Its 2021 estimate put the population at 75.5 percent American Indian and Alaska Native. The 2020 census counted 72,902 residents, down from 74,798 in 2000, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 68,119.

Most residents therefore live outside Gallup, in census-designated places such as Thoreau, Tohatchi, Church Rock, Ramah, Pinehaven and Zuni Pueblo. The Census Bureau lists 44 such places in the county, so the first step for any property here is pinning down exactly which jurisdiction it sits in.

sections.h2: Why does land ownership matter when selling a McKinley County house?
sections.html:
It decides which rules apply, because land inside the reservations is not all taxed or transferred the way private land is. The Bureau of Indian Affairs states that trust land is not subject to state or local taxes, although tribes may tax it to support their own services.

The Navajo Nation Tax Commission separately describes a possessory interest tax, a tax on the right to be on Navajo land for a particular activity such as an oil and gas lease, a right-of-way or a business site lease. Fee land, meaning ordinary privately owned land with a deed, stays under county rules.

  • Fee land with a recorded deed is assessed by the McKinley County Assessor and billed by the Treasurer.
  • Trust land and tribal land assignments follow tribal and federal procedures.
  • Before you price or advertise, confirm whether your land is fee, trust, or held by lease or assignment.

The assessor's records and the county clerk's recorded documents are the quickest way to tell fee land from other holdings. A title company will ask the same question first.

sections.h2: What does the McKinley County economy rest on?
sections.html:
Schools, health care, travel and tribal government do much of the work, and Gallup's position on Interstate 40 feeds a travel trade. The state labor department lists Gallup-McKinley County Schools, Gallup Indian Medical Center and Rehoboth McKinley Christian Health Care Services among the large employers.

Local attractions it names include Fort Wingate, the Gallup Cultural Center, Red Rock State Park and the Inter-Tribal Indian Ceremonial. Part of Chaco Culture National Historical Park and part of the Cibola National Forest lie inside the county. Highways include I-40, with a business loop through Gallup, and US 491.

Water has been a long-running constraint. The Bureau of Reclamation's Navajo-Gallup Water Supply Project is designed to carry municipal and industrial water from the San Juan River to the eastern Navajo Nation, part of the Jicarilla Apache Nation and Gallup.

Schools: Gallup-McKinley County Schools run most public schools, among them Gallup High, Miyamura High, Crownpoint High, Thoreau High and Tohatchi High. The Zuni Public School District serves the Zuni area, and the Bureau of Indian Education operates schools near Fort Wingate and in Pueblo Pintado.

sections.h2: Which McKinley County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
The McKinley County Assessor lists and values taxable property, and the McKinley County Treasurer collects. The treasurer's page says the office collects taxes, penalties and interest under the Property Tax Code, Sections 7-35-1 through 7-38-90 NMSA 1978.

The county also publishes charts of taxes billed by taxing entity for each tax year, which show how a bill divides among county, school and other districts. Those charts show amounts billed, not amounts collected. Start at the treasurer's page and the assessor's page.

sections.h2: What are the McKinley County property tax deadlines?
sections.html:
McKinley County uses the state calendar, with payments due November 10 and April 10. A New Mexico Taxation and Revenue schedule sets these steps for every county.

  • January 1: property is valued as of this date, and the tax lien attaches.
  • September 1: the state Department of Finance and Administration sets rates.
  • November 1: treasurers send bills.
  • November 10 and December 10: the first half is due, and interest starts after December 10.
  • April 10 and May 10: the second half is due, and interest starts after May 10.
  • January 10 of the following year: last day to file a refund claim in district court.

Interest on late payments runs at 1 percent a month, according to the scorecard the state department presented to legislators. Because the lien is a first lien under Section 7-38-48, ahead of any other interest, an unpaid McKinley County bill follows the house to whoever owns it next.

sections.h2: How is a McKinley County house valued for tax?
sections.html:
The assessor values it at current and correct value as of January 1, then applies the residential cap. Taxable value is one third of that figure. Residential assessments cannot rise more than 3 percent a year unless the property changes ownership, is improved or is rezoned.

The Census Bureau figures on this page's header show a median home value of $72,100 in McKinley County, well below the state midpoint. Lower values mean smaller absolute bills, but the rules do not change: a late payment still draws interest, and a delinquent account still ends up at the state.

Two details matter in a sale. A change of ownership removes the cap, so the buyer's first valuation is a fresh one. And the $2,000 head of family exemption belongs to a resident's primary home and is removed when ownership changes. A transfer to a child who occupies the home as a principal residence, or into a revocable trust for the owner's spouse or child, is excluded from the definition of change of ownership.

sections.h2: What can a McKinley County owner do about a high valuation?
sections.html:
File a written petition with the assessor within 30 days of the mailing of the notice of valuation, or by April 1, whichever is later. Protests go to a county valuation protest board, which includes one member from the state's Appraisal Bureau.

A timely protest keeps the disputed part of the tax from becoming delinquent. The other route is to pay first and file a refund claim in district court. The scorecard in the state's 2024 legislative presentation shows no fee for an initial protest, and the department publishes a protest pamphlet.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid McKinley County property tax?
sections.html:
After three full years of delinquency, the account moves to the state's Delinquent Property Tax Bureau, which can sell the property at public auction. Before that, the bureau tries phone calls, certified mail, site visits and notices left on the property, and it offers installment agreements.

If an auction sale brings more than the tax, penalty, interest and costs, the remainder goes to the former owner. State law requires an auction in each county every year, so McKinley County is not an exception.

  • Heirs who inherit a house on fee land should check the treasurer's account before listing.
  • Owners who moved away should confirm the treasurer has a current mailing address.

sections.h2: How does a quick sale usually work in McKinley County?
sections.html:
The seller proves ownership, clears any tax lien, and signs a deed that is recorded with the county clerk. Under Section 14-9-3 NMSA 1978, an unrecorded deed does not affect title against a later purchaser, so recording protects the buyer.

If a house has an estate attached, the probate steps come first. New Mexico's court self-help guide says an estate with real property cannot use the small-estate affidavit, and a personal representative's deed may be needed to move title out of the decedent's name.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in McKinley County, NM?
faqs.a: The McKinley County Treasurer, at 207 W Hill Ave, Suite 101, in Gallup, phone (505) 722-4459. The office is open 8 AM to 5 PM, Monday through Friday.

faqs.q: When are McKinley County property taxes due?
faqs.a: November 10 for the first half and April 10 for the second. Interest starts after December 10 and May 10.

faqs.q: Is trust land in McKinley County taxed by the county?
faqs.a: No. The Bureau of Indian Affairs says trust land is not subject to state or local taxes. Tribes may assess their own taxes, such as the Navajo possessory interest tax.

faqs.q: How long do I have to protest my valuation?
faqs.a: You have 30 days from the date the assessor mailed the notice, or until April 1, whichever is later. File the petition with the county assessor.

faqs.q: Does New Mexico have an inheritance tax that affects a McKinley County estate?
faqs.a: No. New Mexico does not impose an inheritance tax, and its estate tax was phased out as of January 1, 2005.

faqs.q: Can I sell a McKinley County house that has delinquent taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The tax has to be paid or settled at closing, because the lien ranks ahead of other interests. Get a payoff figure from the treasurer.
